html:
The Battle of Tannenberg was fought from 26 to 30 August 1914 in East Prussia, now northern Poland. The German Eighth Army surrounded and destroyed the Russian Second Army in the first month of World War I.

Russia invaded East Prussia early to help France, before its armies were ready. Two Russian armies advanced, split apart by the Masurian Lakes. Germany sent Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff to take command. The Russians sent radio orders uncoded, so the Germans knew their plans. Leaving a thin screen in front of the northern army, they moved their troops by rail against the southern one, under Alexander Samsonov, and closed in on both its sides. About 92,000 Russians were taken prisoner and tens of thousands were killed or wounded. Samsonov shot himself.

The Germans named the battle after a nearby village, to answer the defeat of the Teutonic Knights there in 1410; see the Battle of Grunwald. It made Hindenburg a national hero. He later ran the German war effort and, as president, made Hitler chancellor in 1933. But the invasion had made Germany move two army corps east, away from the Marne, and Russia fought on for three more years.
